name: SR9009 (Stenabolic)
lead: SR9009, sold under the name Stenabolic, is a synthetic small molecule that activates REV-ERB, a pair of nuclear receptors (REV-ERBα and REV-ERBβ) that help run the body's circadian clock and regulate metabolism and inflammation. It was developed as a laboratory tool compound and has been studied in cells and animals; it is not an approved medicine anywhere. [3][5][7]

In bodybuilding and fitness forums it is marketed and discussed as an endurance, fat-loss and "SARM-adjacent" product, often stacked with other research compounds such as Cardarine. [11][12][13] Published research, however, classifies it as a REV-ERB agonist rather than a selective androgen receptor modulator, and the evidence base consists of preclinical studies in rodents and cell lines. [3][4][7]

No published human clinical trial has tested SR9009 for fat loss, endurance or muscle. A 2025 case report described drug-induced liver injury in a man who had started a product sold as Stenabolic, and several studies have reported effects of SR9009 that appear independent of REV-ERB, complicating interpretation of the animal data. [7][8][9][10]

paras: SR9009 has no approved medical use. In research settings it has been used to probe the role of REV-ERB in circadian biology, metabolism, inflammation and cancer cell biology. [1][3][6][20]

In the fitness and bodybuilding market it is sold under the name Stenabolic and promoted for endurance, fat reduction and as an addition to anabolic or SARM "stacks". T Nation forum users describe taking it alongside testosterone and other anabolic agents while trying to reduce body fat, and others discuss combining it with Cardarine for endurance training. [11][12][13][14]

SR9009 binds and activates REV-ERBα and REV-ERBβ, which repress transcription of clock and metabolic genes. Reviews describe REV-ERB agonists, including SR9009, SR9011 and SR12418, as suppressing Th17 cell differentiation and reducing disease severity in preclinical autoimmune models. [4] A review of circadian drugs lists SR9009 alongside tasimelteon and ramelteon, and notes that REV-ERBα drives the morning surge in platelet reactivity in the mechanistic work it summarises. [3]

Not all reported effects appear to depend on the target receptor. A 2019 study reported REV-ERB-independent effects of SR9009 on cell proliferation and metabolism, a 2022 study reported that it improved heart function after pressure overload independent of cardiac REV-ERB, and a 2021 study reported that it activates NRF2 to counteract cellular senescence. [8][9][10] A forum post on T Nation gives the half-life as roughly four to five hours, which is a user-reported figure rather than a published pharmacokinetic result. [18]

No studies found in humans for fat loss, endurance, body composition or any other appearance-related use. Published work on SR9009 is preclinical. Examples include mouse studies of weight gain, insulin resistance and white fat accumulation under constant light exposure, a mouse study in which a single day of treatment after myocardial ischemia-reperfusion prevented heart failure, studies of cancer cells and oncogene-induced senescence, and neuroinflammation models. [5][6][20][21][22][23]

A mouse study published in 2018 reported that pharmacological activation of REV-ERBs was lethal to cancer cells and oncogene-induced senescence cells while sparing normal cells in the models used. [20] These findings concern disease models and have not been tested in healthy people seeking a leaner physique. A 2016 review of exercise and caloric restriction "mimetics" noted that such compounds have mostly been described in preclinical settings with limited translation into humans. [2]

Because no human trials exist, the safety profile in people is not established. A 2025 case report in Cureus describes a 40-year-old man who developed drug-induced liver injury after starting a product sold as Stenabolic, which the authors framed as a newer SARM; the authors noted that SARM-related liver injury is rare but potentially serious. [7]

Forum users who combine Stenabolic with anabolic steroids describe monitoring liver enzymes and triglycerides through periodic bloodwork, but in those cases other compounds were being taken at the same time, so effects cannot be attributed to SR9009. [11]

Stenabolic is discussed on T Nation in cycle-planning threads, where it appears in lists with steroids, SARMs and Cardarine, and in questions about how long it stays detectable in the body and how it fits around post-cycle therapy. [11][12][13][15][16][17] Some posters describe it as a SARM, a label also seen in forum discussions comparing it with compounds such as YK-11. [14]
The review literature places it among circadian-targeting compounds rather than androgen receptor ligands. [3]

timeline.event: A Nature paper reports that REV-ERB agonists, including SR9009, are lethal to cancer cells and oncogene-induced senescence cells in preclinical models. [20]
Studies report REV-ERB-independent effects of SR9009 on cell proliferation and metabolism, and anti-inflammatory heart effects in mice. [8][21]
A case report links drug-induced liver injury to a product sold as Stenabolic. [7]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding forums, Stenabolic is discussed as an endurance and fat-loss add-on to steroid or SARM cycles. Threads mostly ask about stacking, cycle length, side effects and drug-test detectability. [11][12][13][15][16]

claims.claim: Stenabolic boosts endurance and helps with cutting body fat
claims.believers: Users describe adding it to cutting cycles to reduce body fat and make abs more visible, and others plan to use it with Cardarine for running and military fitness training. [12][13][14]
claims.experts: No published human study has tested SR9009 for endurance or fat loss; the supporting research is in mice and cell models, and a review notes that exercise-mimetic compounds have mostly not been translated into humans. [2][5]

claims.believers: A T Nation post lists it under the heading of SARMs alongside YK-11. [14]
claims.experts: Scientific literature describes SR9009 as a REV-ERB agonist that acts on circadian clock nuclear receptors, not the androgen receptor. [3][4]

claims.claim: It can be stacked with Cardarine and other SARMs
claims.believers: Posters ask about and report planning Cardarine plus Stenabolic stacks, or a SARM stack with Stenabolic and an anti-estrogen as a precaution. [13][14][19]
claims.experts: No trials have tested these combinations, and published reports of liver injury involve a product sold as Stenabolic. [7]

claims.claim: Stenabolic is gentle enough to run during or after a steroid cycle
claims.believers: Some users plan cycles of a few weeks and ask whether it can be used during post-cycle therapy, treating it as a low-risk addition. [15]
claims.experts: There are no human safety trials, and a case report documents drug-induced liver injury after starting Stenabolic. [7]

claims.claim: The way it works is well understood
claims.believers: Proponents describe it as simply activating a clock receptor to raise energy expenditure.
claims.experts: Studies have reported REV-ERB-independent effects on proliferation, metabolism, cardiac function and senescence, so the mechanism in animals is not settled. [8][9][10]

card.summary: A REV-ERB clock-receptor agonist sold as Stenabolic for endurance and cutting; mouse data only, nothing in humans, and a liver-injury case report.
card.note: Not a SARM despite the label; no human trials; liver injury case reported.

quick.overview:
SR9009 (Stenabolic) is a lab compound that switches on REV-ERB, receptors that tie the body clock to metabolism. It is sold online for endurance and fat loss and is often called a SARM, though research classifies it differently.

All published work is in cells and animals. No human trial has tested it for appearance or performance.
quick.mechanism: It activates REV-ERBα and REV-ERBβ, which repress clock and metabolic genes. Several studies report effects that appear independent of REV-ERB, so its mechanism is not settled.
quick.risks: Human safety is unestablished. A 2025 case report describes liver injury after starting a product sold as Stenabolic. It is not an approved drug, and users often combine it with other compounds, which confounds any reported effects.
